VIDEO.title: Jesus FULFILLS This Promise by Moses! | Ep. 2 (Matthew 2)
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 2 aloud: the magi from the east, Herod's secret meeting, the star leading them to the Child, the gifts, the flight to Egypt, Herod's killing of the boys of Bethlehem, and the return to Nazareth.
He warns against the 'lullaby effect': reading a familiar passage so often that we stop thinking about what it says. Read Matthew 2 with fresh eyes.

Matthew is a Jew writing to Jews, some who follow Jesus and some who do not. He reminds us that Matthew 1 highlighted the outcast, and says chapter 2 tracks along similar lines with Gentile magi coming to worship.

Matthew points to fulfilled prophecy four times: Micah 5:2, Hosea 11:1, Jeremiah 31:15, and 'He shall be called a Nazarene', which he takes as a loose allusion to the prophets, perhaps Jeremiah 23:5 and Jeremiah 33:15.

His big idea: Matthew 2 retells the Exodus. A wicked king kills Hebrew boys, God's son comes out of Egypt, a light guides the way, and the chapter heads toward the wilderness. Jesus is the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15-18), the new Moses who brings a new Exodus and the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:31-34.
QUOTES: It's like the sound of a thousand padlocks all being opened all at once.
The lullaby effect is when we read something that is so familiar to us we stop thinking deeply about what it's saying.
He is the new Moses, and if he's the new Moses, guess what, he's bringing forth a new Exodus.
If Jesus is the fulfillment of promises that God has made to the Israelites, that means he is also the fulfillment of promises that God makes to us all.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Where is He who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw His star in the east and have come to worship Him.

And after coming into the house they saw the Child with Mary His mother; and they fell to the ground and worshiped Him. Then, opening their treasures, they presented to Him gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh.
Yahweh your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers; you shall listen to him.

But this is the covenant which I will cut with the house of Israel after those days, declares Yahweh: I will put My law within them, and on their heart I will write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be My people.

FULFIL.mtText: And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, / Are by no means least among the leaders of Judah; / For out of you shall come forth a Leader / Who will shepherd My people Israel.
FULFIL.otText: But as for you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, / Too little to be among the clans of Judah, / From you One will go forth for Me to be ruler in Israel. / His goings forth are from everlasting, / From the ancient days.
FULFIL.note: The chief priests and scribes answer Herod with this text (2:4-6).

FULFIL.mtText: Out of Egypt I called My Son.
FULFIL.otText: When Israel was a youth I loved him, / And out of Egypt I called My son.
FULFIL.note: In Hosea the 'son' is Israel at the Exodus; Matthew sees Jesus living out Israel's story. The LSB cross-references Exodus 4:22.

FULFIL.mtText: A voice was heard in Ramah, / Weeping and great mourning, / Rachel weeping for her children; / And she was refusing to be comforted, / Because they were no more.
FULFIL.otText: Thus says Yahweh, 'A voice is heard in Ramah, / Wailing and bitter weeping. / Rachel is weeping for her children; / She refuses to be comforted for her children / Because they are no more.'
FULFIL.note: The video urges reading on in Jeremiah 31: the return (v. 16) and the new covenant (vv. 31-34).

FULFIL.mtText: He shall be called a Nazarene.
FULFIL.otText: No single verse says this. Matthew says 'the prophets' (plural). The video suggests a loose allusion, perhaps to the righteous Branch of Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15.
FULFIL.note: See 'Where scholars differ' for the main proposals.

PEOPLE.name: The magi
PEOPLE.video: Gentiles from the East who track a special, divinely appointed star to worship the new King of the Jews, then are warned in a dream to avoid Herod.
PEOPLE.bg: LSB footnote on 2:1: 'A class of wise men specializing in astronomy, astrology, and natural science.' Matthew does not say how many came; 'three' is a later tradition drawn from the three gifts.

PEOPLE.name: Herod the king
PEOPLE.video: A wicked ruler who privately meets the magi so he can find and kill the child; the video calls him a descendant of Esau and not a practicing Jew.
PEOPLE.bg: Herod the Great ruled as Rome's client king of Judea from 37 BC. He was Idumean (Edomite) by descent, and Edom traces back to Esau (Genesis 36:1). He rebuilt the Jerusalem temple on a grand scale.

PEOPLE.name: Joseph
PEOPLE.video: Receives a divine dream warning, takes Mary and Jesus to Egypt, and later brings them back to the land of Israel.
PEOPLE.bg: Joseph is guided by four dreams in Matthew 1-2 (1:20; 2:13; 2:19; 2:22) and obeys each one at once.

PEOPLE.name: Mary
PEOPLE.video: With the Child when the magi arrive and worship.
PEOPLE.bg: Matthew names the Child first each time: 'the Child with Mary His mother' (2:11) and 'the Child and His mother' (2:13, 14, 20, 21).

PEOPLE.name: Chief priests and scribes
PEOPLE.video: Herod gathers them to learn where the Christ is to be born.
PEOPLE.bg: They know the answer from Micah 5:2, yet Matthew records no one from Jerusalem going to Bethlehem with the magi.

PEOPLE.name: Archelaus
PEOPLE.video: Reigning over Judea in place of Herod, so Joseph is afraid to go there.
PEOPLE.bg: A son of Herod, he ruled Judea, Samaria and Idumea from 4 BC until Rome removed him in AD 6.

PEOPLE.name: Rachel
PEOPLE.video: Pictured weeping for her children in Jeremiah 31:15, quoted at Matthew 2:18.
PEOPLE.bg: Jacob's wife, buried 'on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem)' (Genesis 35:19). Ramah is the town where Jerusalem's exiles were held before Babylon (Jeremiah 40:1).

PEOPLE.name: Moses
PEOPLE.video: The pattern Matthew is retelling: the prophet who said God would raise up a prophet like him.
PEOPLE.bg: Moses himself fled from a king who sought to kill him (Exodus 2:15) and was told to return once those seeking his life were dead (Exodus 4:19).

TERMS.def: The video's name for reading a familiar passage so often that we stop thinking about it. The cure: read with fresh eyes.
The video's term for Jewish followers of Jesus who still know and revere the Tanakh and obey Torah.
Tanakh is the Hebrew Bible (our Old Testament); Torah is the Law, the five books of Moses.
The video's key idea: Matthew 2 replays Egyptian cruelty, the Exodus and the wilderness period.
Jeremiah 31:31-34: God's law written on the heart and sins forgiven. The video ties it to the Last Supper.
LSB footnote on 2:1: a class of wise men specializing in astronomy, astrology, and natural science.
Costly aromatic resins from trees of Arabia and the Horn of Africa. Isaiah 60:6 pictures nations bringing 'gold and frankincense.'
Someone from Nazareth, a small Galilean village; see John 1:46, 'Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?'

WORDS.gloss: Magus, one of the magi (LSB note: a class of wise men).
To worship, bow down. The LSB notes 'fell to the ground' in 2:11 as 'Face down in a prone position to indicate worship; lit prostrated.'
Bethlehem, literally 'house of bread' (the video's point).
Branch, shoot (LSB 'branch'). Often proposed as a wordplay behind 'Nazarene' (debated).
Firstborn: 'Israel is My son, My firstborn.'
Star: 'A star shall come forth from Jacob' (an LSB cross-reference for 2:2).

BACKGROUND.p: Herod the Great was Idumean by descent; the Idumeans were the Edomites, Esau's people (Genesis 36:1). Rome named him king, and he held Jerusalem from 37 BC. Ancient sources describe him as a builder (including the temple) and as ruthless toward rivals, even his own sons.

BACKGROUND.h: A visit some time after the birth
BACKGROUND.p: By 2:11 the family is in 'the house', and Herod's cut-off is 'two years old and under' based on what the magi told him (2:7, 16). Many interpreters take this to mean the visit came some months after the birth, not the night of it.

After Herod died, Archelaus ruled Judea while his brother Herod Antipas ruled Galilee. Archelaus' rule was harsh enough that Rome removed him in AD 6. Luke 2:39 also records the family settling in Nazareth.

The video mentions this view. Papias (early 2nd century, quoted by Eusebius) said Matthew compiled the sayings 'in the Hebrew language.' What Papias meant, and how it relates to our Greek Matthew, is debated.
The video cites Acts 15. There the Jerusalem council decides 'that we do not trouble those who are turning to God from among the Gentiles' (Acts 15:19 LSB).

DEBATES.p: No Old Testament verse says this, and Matthew says 'the prophets.' Main proposals: (1) a wordplay on netser, the 'branch' of Isaiah 11:1, with the Branch passages Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15 (close to the video's view); (2) a link to the Nazirite (Judges 13:5); (3) a summary of prophecies that the Messiah would be despised, since Nazareth was looked down on (John 1:46). The views can overlap.

Proposals include a planetary conjunction, a comet, a nova, or a unique supernatural light. Matthew says it went before them and stood over the place where the Child was (2:9), which many take as more than an ordinary star. Numbers 24:17 is an LSB cross-reference.
Matthew says only 'from the east.' Persia, Babylon (with its long tradition of star-watching and a large Jewish community) and Arabia (the gifts; Isaiah 60:6) are all proposed.
Herod's death is usually dated 4 BC, so Jesus' birth is often placed about 6-4 BC. A minority argue Herod died in 1 BC. The date of the Exodus (c. 1446 or the 1260s BC) is also debated.

TIMELINE.what: Rachel dies on the way to Ephrath (Bethlehem); Esau's line becomes Edom
Pharaoh kills Hebrew sons; Moses flees and returns; Israel, God's firstborn son, comes out of Egypt
Pillar of cloud and fire; manna; Balaam's 'star from Jacob'; Moses promises a prophet like him
Hosea: 'out of Egypt I called My son'; Micah: a ruler from Bethlehem
Exiles gathered at Ramah; Jeremiah's comfort and the promise of a new covenant

Herod dies; Archelaus rules Judea; the family settles in Nazareth

QUESTIONS: Fight the lullaby effect: read Matthew 2 slowly, out loud if you can. Which detail had you been reading past without noticing?
Compare Exodus 1:15-22, 2:15 and 4:19 with Matthew 2:13-20. Which parallels stand out, and what would they have told Matthew's Jewish hearers about Jesus?

Gentile magi travel far to worship, while Herod is troubled 'and all Jerusalem with him' (Matthew 2:3). The scribes knew the right verse but did not go. What makes the difference between knowing Scripture and responding to the King?
Read all of Jeremiah 31. How does the hope that follows Rachel's weeping (Jeremiah 31:16-17, 31-34) shape the way you read Matthew 2:18?
The video's assignment: what promises has God made to the nations (for example Genesis 12:3; Isaiah 60:3), and how does Jesus fulfill them for you? What will you do about it this week?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The video's lesson for the original audience: Jesus' birth is not just the story of a savior born in a dramatic moment. It is the fulfillment of many promises God made to His people. Jesus is the prophet like Moses, the new Moses bringing a new Exodus and the new covenant. The same lesson is posed to us: if Jesus fulfills God's promises to Israel, He also fulfills God's promises to us all, so learn what God has promised the nations. The teacher asks each viewer to work out the lesson for their own life and to decide what to do about it.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): Matthew 2 opens with Gentiles from the east worshiping the King of the Jews (Matthew 2:2, 11), an early picture of the nations coming to His light (Isaiah 60:3). The Gospel ends with the risen Jesus sending His disciples to 'make disciples of all the nations' (Matthew 28:19). The promise to Abraham that 'in you all the families of the earth will be blessed' (Genesis 12:3) is kept in Jesus.

CAREFUL: The video once says 'Jeremiah 31:1'; the verse Matthew quotes is Jeremiah 31:15, which the video names later.
The video places 'He shall be called a Nazarene' at Matthew 2:22; it is Matthew 2:23.
The video describes Herod killing 'male firstborns'; Matthew 2:16 says 'all the male children... from two years old and under.'
In one spot the video says Joseph hid 'from Pharaoh'; Matthew 2:13 has Herod. The slip shows how strongly the teacher hears the Exodus in the story.

- Completed Jews: The video's term for Jewish followers of Jesus who still know and revere the Tanakh and obey Torah. (video)
- Tanakh / Torah: Tanakh is the Hebrew Bible (our Old Testament); Torah is the Law, the five books of Moses. (video)
- Exodus motif: The video's key idea: Matthew 2 replays Egyptian cruelty, the Exodus and the wilderness period. (video)
- New covenant: Jeremiah 31:31-34: God's law written on the heart and sins forgiven. The video ties it to the Last Supper. (video)

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Herod's family and power: Herod the Great was Idumean by descent; the Idumeans were the Edomites, Esau's people (Genesis 36:1). Rome named him king, and he held Jerusalem from 37 BC. Ancient sources describe him as a builder (including the temple) and as ruthless toward rivals, even his own sons.
- A visit some time after the birth: By 2:11 the family is in 'the house', and Herod's cut-off is 'two years old and under' based on what the magi told him (2:7, 16). Many interpreters take this to mean the visit came some months after the birth, not the night of it.
- Archelaus and Galilee: After Herod died, Archelaus ruled Judea while his brother Herod Antipas ruled Galilee. Archelaus' rule was harsh enough that Rome removed him in AD 6. Luke 2:39 also records the family settling in Nazareth.
- Did Matthew write in Hebrew?: The video mentions this view. Papias (early 2nd century, quoted by Eusebius) said Matthew compiled the sayings 'in the Hebrew language.' What Papias meant, and how it relates to our Greek Matthew, is debated.
- Jewish and Gentile disciples: The video cites Acts 15. There the Jerusalem council decides 'that we do not trouble those who are turning to God from among the Gentiles' (Acts 15:19 LSB).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- 'He shall be called a Nazarene': No Old Testament verse says this, and Matthew says 'the prophets.' Main proposals: (1) a wordplay on netser, the 'branch' of Isaiah 11:1, with the Branch passages Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15 (close to the video's view); (2) a link to the Nazirite (Judges 13:5); (3) a summary of prophecies that the Messiah would be despised, since Nazareth was looked down on (John 1:46). The views can overlap.
- What was the star?: Proposals include a planetary conjunction, a comet, a nova, or a unique supernatural light. Matthew says it went before them and stood over the place where the Child was (2:9), which many take as more than an ordinary star. Numbers 24:17 is an LSB cross-reference.
- Where were the magi from?: Matthew says only 'from the east.' Persia, Babylon (with its long tradition of star-watching and a large Jewish community) and Arabia (the gifts; Isaiah 60:6) are all proposed.
- Dates: Herod's death is usually dated 4 BC, so Jesus' birth is often placed about 6-4 BC. A minority argue Herod died in 1 BC. The date of the Exodus (c. 1446 or the 1260s BC) is also debated.

## Careful reading notes
- The video once says 'Jeremiah 31:1'; the verse Matthew quotes is Jeremiah 31:15, which the video names later.
- The video places 'He shall be called a Nazarene' at Matthew 2:22; it is Matthew 2:23.
- The video describes Herod killing 'male firstborns'; Matthew 2:16 says 'all the male children... from two years old and under.'
- In one spot the video says Joseph hid 'from Pharaoh'; Matthew 2:13 has Herod. The slip shows how strongly the teacher hears the Exodus in the story.

## Timeline [Background; early dates approximate]
- Patriarchal era: Rachel dies on the way to Ephrath (Bethlehem); Esau's line becomes Edom (Genesis 35-36)
- c. 1446 or 1260s BC: Pharaoh kills Hebrew sons; Moses flees and returns; Israel, God's firstborn son, comes out of Egypt (Exodus 1-4) | Echo: Matthew 2:13-20 | date debated
- Wilderness period: Pillar of cloud and fire; manna; Balaam's 'star from Jacob'; Moses promises a prophet like him (Deuteronomy 18)
- 8th century BC: Hosea: 'out of Egypt I called My son'; Micah: a ruler from Bethlehem (Micah 5) | Quoted: Matthew 2:6, 15
- c. 586 BC: Exiles gathered at Ramah; Jeremiah's comfort and the promise of a new covenant (Jeremiah 31) | Quoted: Matthew 2:18
- 37 BC: Herod the Great takes Jerusalem and rules as king of Judea (Matthew 2)
- c. 6-4 BC: Jesus born in Bethlehem; the magi come; the flight to Egypt (Matthew 2) | Matthew 2:1-15 | date debated
- 4 BC (usual date): Herod dies; Archelaus rules Judea; the family settles in Nazareth (Matthew 2) | Matthew 2:19-23 | date debated
- AD 6: Rome removes Archelaus (Luke 2)

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Fight the lullaby effect: read Matthew 2 slowly, out loud if you can. Which detail had you been reading past without noticing?
2. Compare Exodus 1:15-22, 2:15 and 4:19 with Matthew 2:13-20. Which parallels stand out, and what would they have told Matthew's Jewish hearers about Jesus?
3. Gentile magi travel far to worship, while Herod is troubled 'and all Jerusalem with him' (Matthew 2:3). The scribes knew the right verse but did not go. What makes the difference between knowing Scripture and responding to the King?
4. Read all of Jeremiah 31. How does the hope that follows Rachel's weeping (Jeremiah 31:16-17, 31-34) shape the way you read Matthew 2:18?
5. The video's assignment: what promises has God made to the nations (for example Genesis 12:3; Isaiah 60:3), and how does Jesus fulfill them for you? What will you do about it this week?

## Application
The video's lesson for the original audience: Jesus' birth is not just the story of a savior born in a dramatic moment. It is the fulfillment of many promises God made to His people. Jesus is the prophet like Moses, the new Moses bringing a new Exodus and the new covenant. The same lesson is posed to us: if Jesus fulfills God's promises to Israel, He also fulfills God's promises to us all, so learn what God has promised the nations. The teacher asks each viewer to work out the lesson for their own life and to decide what to do about it.

Study note (added): Matthew 2 opens with Gentiles from the east worshiping the King of the Jews (Matthew 2:2, 11), an early picture of the nations coming to His light (Isaiah 60:3). The Gospel ends with the risen Jesus sending His disciples to 'make disciples of all the nations' (Matthew 28:19). The promise to Abraham that 'in you all the families of the earth will be blessed' (Genesis 12:3) is kept in Jesus.
